Some of you all know I worked in home sales for the better part of a decade.

Got bored last night, had a quick brainstorming session with my Grok Bot, and built Mortgage Unpacked.  

It's a free mortgage resource that has everything mortgage related I could think of, and teaches potential homeowners to look at their situation like an underwriter, breaks down the different types of loans, the steps of mortgage, etc.

I probably should've recorded it, because it literally was as basic as it could be, and I didn't touch one line of code.  

Actually, I never left the Grok Bot app.

I told me Chief of Staff (Ares - Master Control, I'm a massive Tron nerd) what I wanted to do.  Started throwing all the material I wanted to cover and asked him if there was anything obvious that I was missing and he made some recommendations.

Had him create a new bot responsible for the site, Fannie - Mortgage Site Boss.

She did the research, started the build, and sent me her first draft.  It was absolutely horrible, so I told her to clean it up and after a few iterations, I was happy enough.

They're already connected to my domain registrar, so I brainstormed a few name ideas with Ares, settled on one I liked, told him to go buy it and have Fannie push it live.

Once it was live, I found a few things I left out, sent it back to Ares (who sent it to Fannie), told him once she makes the changes and tests it, push it live.  

It's not that elaborate of a site - it dynamically pulls rates - but lots of information and I thought it'd make a great resource for anyone thinking about real estate, realtors, etc.  

All in, under 90 minutes (would've been way faster but I was doing a few other things).

I'm going to do all of this from scratch on a video - should have time tomorrow.

If you want to check it out (whether you're thinking about a morgage or just curious to see what my bots and I put together), check out the link below.

I made Grok Bot our full-time travel assistant for a week-long family road trip. It felt like having someone else working for us while we took care of the kids and enjoyed the trip.

Munich → Nancy → Reims → Disneyland Paris → Paris → Colmar → home, in our Tesla. Two adults, an 8-year-old, and a baby about to turn one.

I'll skip the trip diary. Here's what the bot actually handled.

Planning around my wife
My wife had never been to Paris, so the bot built the week around her: a must-see Paris day, plus two Disney days for the kids. Everything lived on one live day-by-day page with the route map, Supercharger stops, a to-do list and official links. It emailed her a summary in Spanish. She replied the same day: looks great, don't change a thing.

Where we slept
For our two overnight stops, it sent her a shortlist in Spanish: 4 options per city, Airbnbs included, with prices, ratings, cancellation terms and nearby Superchargers. She booked straight from that list. Both places were great.

Grok in the car knew the plan
Grok in my Tesla could reach everything Grok Bot had planned, so I had the whole trip with me in the driver's seat.

Nancy, after 10 p.m.
This is the moment that got me. Weeks earlier, the bot had emailed the hotel in French and learned two things: reception closes at 21:00, and late arrivals have to call the night staff from the gate.

We rolled in after 10 p.m. and the gate was shut. Grok Bot handed the number to Grok in the car, which called right away.

I never touched my phone 🤯

Fighter jets over the Supercharger
While we were charging in Saint-Dizier, dozens of fighter jets roared over us at very low altitude. It was loud enough that my daughter got scared, and we had no idea what was going on. So we asked Grok in the car. It told us we were right next to one of France's most important air bases and that the jets were most likely Rafales on a routine exercise. Then it gave us a little lecture on the Rafale and fighter jets in general. The scary moment ended up as a lesson for the whole car.

Lunch in Reims
It searched the Michelin Guide for a good restaurant on our route and under our budget, and found Brasserie Le Jardin in Reims. Then it made the reservation itself, in French, added a high chair for the baby and moved us from 12:30 to 13:30. When we were still running late on the road, it told them we'd arrive around 14:00.

Disney
It researched the best place to watch the closing show and found us the perfect spot.

A new plan for Paris
We changed plans on Paris day, so the bot rebuilt it around an afternoon and evening: a garage at Porte Maillot, the metro to the Louvre and the Tuileries, Notre-Dame, the Champs-Élysées, then Trocadéro for sunset and the Eiffel Tower sparkle. It emailed my wife the new plan in Spanish, with walking maps.

Colmar in the rain
Driving to Colmar in the rain, we were going to miss reception. The bot fixed our booking and arranged a key-safe check-in.

The next morning it rebuilt the day:
• the best parking
• the little green train instead of the boat (grey day + baby)
• the toy museum
• a brunch spot with specialty coffee
• a self-guided Little Venice walk with a Google Maps route

My inbox
It checked my email every morning and evening and only pinged me when something needed a decision. It flagged important receipts and deadlines and left the rest alone.

Spanish for my wife
My wife and I plan in Spanish, so the bot wrote to her in Spanish and answered her questions about parking and checkout.

People here show Grok Bot automating their work. I used it to carry the logistics of a family trip, so we could spend the week with the kids and with each other.

I’ve been working with Grok Bot for several weeks and have recently detected serious flaws. 

It has major memory problems and gets confused with simple instructions, even though it handles complex operations well. 

I’ve put real effort into building a robust memory system with dedicated folders for each bot, and the result is still mediocre. 

Processing is low. Today has been especially bad. We’re building a relatively simple application and it repeats mistakes over and over.

The worst part is that when the application is already working correctly and only detail adjustments remain, correcting them destroys all the previous work. It does this constantly. The errors are unacceptable. 

Grok Bot is astonishingly powerful, but these failures cannot be tolerated. They should improve the memory system. My bots have very specific instructions and they break them repeatedly.

This is not an isolated glitch. It is the consequence of a design that prioritizes impressing in demos over being reliable in daily use. 

The external memory system I built is a patch on top of another patch. 

The problem is not in my folders, but in how the model weighs what it reads against what it internally assumes it already knows. 

That is why it breaks concrete instructions: it is not that it does not understand them, it is that it subordinates them to an internal assumption I cannot audit. https://t.co/V2LuHDig19

note_tweet.text:
Larry's Desk Series 7 of 10
These are long, send to your agent.

THE PROMISE:
By the end of this post you will:
1. Know the 4 steps on https://t.co/U2UEFCcJMV and what each one does on a Mac.
2. Know what the first prompt asks the agent to do, including the one change it makes before it asks you anything.
3. Hear the 3 design ideas I threw out of that page, and why each one got dropped.
4. Get a 5 step checklist for vetting any one-command onboarding page.
5. Get a read-only prompt that does the vetting for you.

On October 20 I posted: "Most AI setup guides hand you 10 commands. Mine hands you 1 paste. Install Claude Code. Paste 1 prompt." Then I built the page that proves it, and cut most of what I first put on it.

Larry is my Claude Code agent. Lots of people have asked me to build them their own. My guide, https://t.co/58oMuKU6yL, has the whole answer in dozens of chapters, which is the wrong size for someone who has never seen a blinking cursor. So on October 22 I built https://t.co/U2UEFCcJMV, a Mac only on-ramp with one job: get a complete beginner to a first real conversation with their own agent. Not a finished AI. A first conversation.

THE 4 STEPS ON THE PAGE

The page opens with a banner that stays on screen: free guide, and Claude plan separate. Claude Code needs a paid Claude plan, and the page says so before you scroll, not in a footnote.

Step 1: open Terminal. Press Command and Space, type Terminal, press Return. It is already on your Mac.

Step 2: install Claude Code with one command, copied from a button. That is Anthropic's own installer, from Anthropic's own quickstart:

curl -fsSL https://t.co/hedZawlFh1 | bash

Step 3: make a folder, start Claude Code in it, and sign in with your Claude account in a browser:

mkdir -p ~/nixfredOS && cd ~/nixfredOS && ~/.local/bin/claude

Step 4: paste the first prompt. The button copies one sentence asking for help building your own AI, one step at a time, in simple words, with you choosing its name. The complete prompt is also at a plain text link, so a skeptic can read all of it first. Next time, open Terminal, go to that folder and run claude with --continue to pick up the last conversation.

The folder, the login and the conversation all live on your Mac.

WHAT THE FIRST PROMPT ASKS YOUR AGENT TO DO

It connects my guide to Claude Code through its MCP server, which is a single line added to your Claude Code configuration. That is the one change it makes before asking you anything. After that it checks what you already have, builds the foundation in order, and asks before installing anything or touching your files. It never deletes or overwrites an existing setup without your permission, it treats the guide as reference material and not orders, and it says so when it doesn't know something. When the foundation works, it picks one small useful thing for the two of you to do.

WRONG IDEA 1: A PROGRESS BAR

The idea: an onboarding page should show how far along you are. The first version had a checkbox on each step, a bar reading "0 of 4 steps checked," saved in your browser, and a "first win" panel when all 4 were ticked.

Why it seemed smart: every onboarding flow has one, and a filling bar feels like progress.

Why it didn't hold: a bar that fills to 100 percent tells a beginner they are building something that finishes. Step 4 finishes. The AI never does. I was promising a finish line I couldn't deliver.

What replaced it: nothing, on purpose. The checkboxes, the counter and the panel are gone, and the page's own README now says it promises a first conversation, not a completed personal AI in 4 steps.

WRONG IDEA 2: SELL THE DREAM, HIDE THE COST

The idea: lead with the possibility, in a soft light theme. The first headline was "A little help. A lot more possibility." and the first paragraph began "Imagine an AI that gets to know you." The note about the paid plan sat in a small box mid page, and the chat sat in its own section below the steps.

Why it seemed smart: dreams sell. I wanted people excited before I showed them the work.

Why it didn't hold: a beginner is not stuck on the dream. They are stuck on where Terminal is, what this costs and who to ask. Help you find only after you are stuck is not help.

What replaced it: the headline became "Your own AI. One step at a time." The cost moved into the banner that never scrolls away. The chat became a column that stays open beside the steps, docked at the bottom on a phone. Tell a beginner what to do, what it costs and where help is, all on the first screen.

WRONG IDEA 3: A COPY BUTTON THAT FETCHES ON CLICK

The idea: the first prompt lives in one file, the single source for both the button and the plain text link. So the first copy button fetched that file when you clicked it, then copied it.

Why it seemed smart: one source of truth, nothing duplicated.

Why it didn't hold: on a Mac, which is exactly the wrong audience to fail, browsers only allow a clipboard write for a short window after your click, and a fetch that finishes later misses it. The button looked like it worked and copied nothing.

What replaced it: the page loads the prompt up front. If you click before it has arrived, it tells you the prompt is ready and asks for a second click, instead of failing silently. The one gesture your whole page depends on can't wait on anything. And I kept the plain text link, because a copy button is a convenience, not a guarantee.

VET ANY ONE-COMMAND PAGE: 5 STEPS

1. Write down each command the page asks you to paste, in plain words. If you can't say what one does, don't paste it.
2. For a command that pipes a download into a shell, download it and read it first, with curl -fsSL https://t.co/hedZawlFh1 -o https://t.co/G9g8YKj8GP, then open the file. Nothing runs until you run it.

note_tweet.text:
Grok Bot is replaceable.

I say that as someone who runs a lot of my days on it.

I'm moving my bots over to OpenBot one by one and testing both side by side every day. So far, my daily routine carries over. Honestly, it could carry over to almost any AI agent.

What I'll miss is real: the big team behind Grok Bot, and how constantly it keeps improving. That can be rebuilt, but only slowly.

The bigger difference turned out to be the model.

A model I pay for on my own subscription is one I can use however I want, without the anxiety of losing my daily routines.

The platform matters less than I thought. The model I choose matters more.

If the tool running your routines disappeared tomorrow, what would you still own?
